Senses.PreferredTarget: knowing hot and cold for oneself
AlternateTargets: one knows the water's temperature for oneself
Senses.Explanation: Literally, one knows (自知) cold and warmth (冷暖) for oneself, usually in the comparison “like a person drinking water, knowing hot and cold for himself” (如人飲水冷暖自知). Huiming uses it after Huineng's instruction to report that he now has an entry; Huangbo joins it to conduct in each movement, dwelling, and instant; and other teachers pair it with looking for oneself rather than seeking from another. The phrase also becomes an object of interrogation: Longmen Foyan grants that hot and cold can be known, then asks what the one who knows for himself is. Daodu pairs “knowing hot and cold for oneself” with “handling slow and urgent matters for oneself” and says the matter cannot be spoken out even when both parties exert themselves. The Chan bend is this sensory commonplace's use as a first-person report, an answer about the Way, and a question about the knower; the texts preserve the water comparison and these recorded deployments.
Senses.Note: The corpus has 68 exact occurrences in 54 allowlisted files. The full water comparison occurs widely; variants reverse the order or substitute a fish drinking water. Distinct deployments include Huiming's report, Huangbo's instruction, a self-versus-other contrast, Daodu's paired formula, and Foyan's corrective question.

Occurrences.Kwic: 今蒙行者指授，也有入處，如人飲水冷暖自知。從今向後，行者即是慧明師
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Huiming reports to Huineng that he now has an entry, like a person drinking water and knowing hot and cold for himself.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一等學禪莫取次𡚶生異見如人飲水冷暖自知一行一住一剎那間念念不異
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Huangbo joins the water comparison to each movement, dwelling, and instant without difference.

Occurrences.Kwic: 智與理冥境與神會時如人飲水冷暖自知遂自思惟冷暖則可矣作麼生是自知底事無不深疑
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Foyan hears the water formula, accepts knowing hot and cold, then deeply doubts and asks what the one that knows for itself is.

Occurrences.Kwic: 應須自家看取，莫向他人所求。不見道，如人上山，各自努力；如人飲水，冷暖自知。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A lamp record contrasts looking for oneself with seeking from another and gives the water comparison alongside each person exerting himself while climbing a mountain.

Occurrences.Kwic: 此事元沒有愛憎，彼此盡力道不出底，只是冷暖自知、緩急自辦
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Daodu says both parties cannot speak the matter out and pairs knowing hot and cold oneself with handling slow and urgent matters oneself.

Senses.PreferredTarget: a bean pops in cold ashes
AlternateTargets: a bean bursts in cold ash
Senses.Explanation: Literally, “a bean pops in cold ashes.” The image occurs 47 times in 37 allowlisted texts, chiefly in seventeenth-century Chan records. Its recorded neighbors make the image concrete: “the cold furnace has no smoke; a bean pops in cold ashes” (寒爐煙絕，冷灰豆爆); a public question asks, “leaving aside a withered tree flowering, what about when a bean pops in cold ashes?” and receives “a thunderclap on level ground” (平地一聲雷). Other addresses follow the phrase with impossible growth—stone bamboo shoots sprout, flame comes from an icy river, an iron tree flowers, and a wooden man claps—or simply with “suddenly, one sound” (驀地一聲). The corpus also speaks of “a person in whom a bean has popped in cold ashes” (冷灰豆爆底人), making the image an appraisal in an interview. Zen bends a domestic image of an unlikely pop from spent ash into a stock address and interview phrase, repeatedly paired with sound and impossible renewal. Those pairings are the texts’ own; this entry assigns no hidden event to the image.
Senses.Note: Event phrase, attributive person-label, and poetic heading all retain the same cold-ash image. They do not name different things. The family comparison with “dead ashes” (死灰), “cold ashes” (寒灰), and “a withered tree flowers” (枯木開花) supports the contrast visible in the passages but not an imported psychological explanation.

Occurrences.Kwic: 忽有箇冷灰豆爆底人到來，如何接待？
上善拼命必死，壁立萬仞，縣崖撒手，及第還鄉；中善寒爐煙絕，冷灰豆爆，親知下落；下善步步踏著實地
設若今日冷灰豆爆，便見條抽石筍，燄吐冰河，鐵樹開華，木人撫掌。
一朝冷灰豆爆，驀地一聲，管取現成受用。
師問眾：「枯木開花即不問，冷灰豆爆時如何？」定侍者云：「平地一聲雷。」

AlternateTargets: Deshan goes down with his bowl
Senses.Explanation: A case title, literally 'Deshan carries his bowl.' It occurs 115 times in 41 allowlisted texts. The case records Deshan going down with his bowl before bell or drum; Xuefeng asks where he is going, Deshan returns to his quarters, Xuefeng reports this to Yantou, and Yantou says Deshan has not understood the last phrase. Deshan summons Yantou, who privately states his meaning; the next day's ascent of the seat differs from usual, and Yantou says Deshan will live only three more years. The corpus turns this named encounter into a case heading, verse topic, question asked at the teaching seat, assigned object of inquiry, and point of later prose comment. Recorded replies to 'what is its meaning?' include 'no meaning' followed by 'if he wanted to go, he went; if he wanted to sit, he sat,' and, elsewhere, 'buying dear and selling cheap.'
Senses.Note: The Zen deviation is institutional: an ordinary meal-bowl movement becomes the fixed public name of a multi-speaker case, repeatedly raised, questioned, versified, and assigned for inquiry. The corpus's divergent later comments are reported as comments, not combined into an interpretation of Deshan's intent. The title and descriptions name the same encounter and require one sense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 德山托鉢德山一日托鉢下堂。見雪峯問者。老漢鐘未鳴鼓未響。托鉢向甚處去。山便回方丈。峯舉似巖頭。頭云。大小德山未會末後句。山聞。令侍者喚巖頭來。問曰。汝不肯老僧那。巖頭密啟其意。山乃休去。明日陞座。果與尋常不同。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Wumen Guan preserves the case's action and speaker sequence.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問。德山托鉢意旨如何。師云。無意旨。進云。因什麼托鉢下僧堂。師云。要行便行。要坐便坐。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A teaching-seat exchange asks the case's meaning and records the answer 'no meaning.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問。德山托鉢歸方丈。意旨如何。師云。貴買賤賣。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Another public exchange names the return to the quarters and answers 'buying dear and selling cheap.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 悅因舉德山托鉢話令熟究之，公悵然不寐，至五鼓，忽垂脚飜溺器，猛省
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A lamp biography records the case being assigned for sustained inquiry.

Occurrences.Kwic: 德山托鉢托鉢無言方丈去，諸方慢謂失便宜，不是巖頭傍著眼，從教後代逐狐疑。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later verse treats the case under its fixed title and explicitly names Yantou's intervention and later doubt.

Senses.Explanation: Literally ‘Deshan's staff/blows,’ the compound that later Chan records pair with ‘Linji's shout’ (臨濟喝). Its contexts use the object-and-blow polysemy of ‘staff/blow’ (棒) rather than choosing only one side: device lists can name the implement as Deshan's staff, while ‘under Deshan's blows’ (德山棒下) records Xuefeng receiving the striking action. Later masters raise the pair as a public question—‘Linji's shout seldom meets one who knows its sound; Deshan's staff rarely meets an adept’—and ask what matter the two clarify. Other records call the paired devices a model left for Chan people, praise or criticize them, and compare Deshan's blows to falling rain. The compound therefore names Deshan's celebrated striking device as both implement and delivered blow; unlike bare ‘staff/blow’ (棒), these are two grammatically available faces of one named Deshan formula, not two independently functioning dictionary referents.
Senses.Note: 490 hits in 173 allowlist files in the b025 preflight. The entry cross-checks bare ‘staff/blow’ (棒) and its established object/blow split: staff-bearing catalogues license ‘Deshan's staff,’ while ‘under the blows’ (棒下) and rain-like striking license ‘Deshan's blows.’ Preferred English uses the act because the strongest case-level witness is Xuefeng under the blows, while the object rendering remains explicit. Do not attribute every later answer or appraisal to Deshan himself.

Occurrences.Kwic: 我當時在德山棒下。如桶底脫相似。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu quotes Xuefeng's report: under Deshan's blows it was like the bottom falling out of a bucket. This anchors the act side of ‘staff/blow’ (棒).

Occurrences.Kwic: 臨濟喝，德山棒，留與禪人作模範。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later master lists Linji's shout and Deshan's staff as models left for Chan people.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問：臨濟喝少遇知音，德山棒難逢作者。和尚今日作麼生？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk raises the paired formula in a public question, saying Deshan's staff rarely meets an adept.

Occurrences.Kwic: 德山棒、臨濟喝，是三世諸佛慈悲喜捨之樂。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later sermon appraises Deshan's staff and Linji's shout together as the joy of the buddhas' kindness, compassion, joy, and generosity; this is the text's appraisal, not the dictionary's.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問德山棒臨濟喝未審明得什麼邊事師云你試道看僧便喝
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk asks what side of the matter Deshan's staff and Linji's shout clarify; the master demands that he say, and the monk shouts.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, to sever an arm. In the Chan record it overwhelmingly names the founding episode in which Shenguang, later named Huike, stands in the snow before Bodhidharma, cuts off his left arm, and places it before him. The lamp account has Bodhidharma say, 'you have now cut off your arm before me; your seeking may be accepted,' and then rename him Huike. Later records compress the episode into paired formulas—'standing in the snow and cutting off the arm,' 'cutting off the arm and pacifying the mind,' or 'face the wall for nine years / cut off the arm and pacify the mind'—and repeatedly reopen it as a public question. One master asks, 'what did the cutting off of the arm accomplish?' and strikes the staff before leaving the seat. Another is asked why one cuts off an arm to seek the Way if this house style is inherent in everyone; he replies, 'there are many mistaken understandings.' Still another says, 'why cut off an arm and seek elsewhere?' The Chan-specific bend is that Huike's bodily act becomes compact lineage and interview language, quoted, challenged, and criticized across later records. These later uses do not authorize this entry to declare the act a required sacrifice or explain its intention beyond what the accounts say.
Senses.Note: Zen-allowlist count: 563 hits in 216 texts. Family check covered standing in the snow (立雪), Shenguang or Huike (神光／慧可), pacifying the mind (安心), seeking the Way or teaching (求道／求法), nine years facing the wall (面壁九年), and the Second Patriarch (二祖). All refer back to the same bodily act; narrative, epithet, and later question are not different things. Names remain contextual because Huike is a lineage patriarch and belongs on the master roster, not as a separate dictionary figure.

Occurrences.Kwic: 自斷左臂。置于祖前。祖知是法器。乃曰。諸佛最初求道。為法忘形。汝今斷臂吾前。求亦可在。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Narrative core: Shenguang cuts off his left arm and places it before Bodhidharma; Bodhidharma acknowledges the act.

Occurrences.Kwic: 有神光法師，立雪斷臂，堅求諸佛要道，師為易名慧可。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Compact lineage formula: Shenguang stands in the snow, cuts off his arm, seeks the essential Way, and is renamed Huike.

Occurrences.Kwic: 少室巖前，祖師斷臂。且道斷臂作箇什麼？卓拄杖一下，下座。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later master asks publicly what cutting off the arm accomplished, strikes the staff, and leaves the seat.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：「者段家風，人人本具，因甚斷臂求道？」師云：「錯會不少。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Public challenge: if this house style is inherent in everyone, why cut off an arm to seek the Way? Reply: 'there are many mistaken understandings.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 一一真常獨露，何須斷臂別求？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Later critical deployment: 'each is openly constant and true—why cut off an arm and seek elsewhere?'

Occurrences.Kwic: 二祖親傳曾斷臂，曾斷臂，血常流，直至而今痛未休。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Verse retrospect: 'the Second Patriarch personally received the transmission and once cut off his arm; the blood still flows, and to this day the pain has not ceased.'

Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'look through' or 'look and break through.' The compound occurs 509 times in 154 allowed texts. It is used transitively of a saying, case, person, condition, or distinction; in passive clauses someone or something is 'seen through.' Hongzhi asks, 'What is the eye with which you can see through it?' (作麼生是儞覷得破底眼). A later address sets out a repeated contrast: 'if you cannot see through it, stand steadily on it, or tread it; if you can see through it, stand steadily on it, and tread it' (若覷不破、立不穩、踏不著；若覷得破，立得穩、踏得著). Comments on earlier cases say that someone saw through Lingyun and Mahakasyapa, that Tianning saw through Dahui, or that an interlocutor should see through an action before it occurs. The passive form appears in a warning about being seen through by someone at a later time (他時異日被人覷破). The fuller form 'be able to see through' (覷得破) occurs 40 times in 25 texts, while the emphatic 'with one look, see through' (一覷覷破) occurs 19 times in 17. The texts do not supply a separate technical definition beyond these observable objects, contrasts, questions, and active/passive constructions.
Senses.Note: The two hits for 'one who sees through this' (覷破者) use the final graph as the pronoun 'this,' not as a definition formula. They were therefore not treated as self-definitions. The corpus range is grammatical rather than polysemous: the same verb occurs with people, words, cases, and named distinctions as its object.

Occurrences.Kwic: 正當十五日。覷破兩頭。直得君臣道合。父子氣和。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Extensive Record of Hongzhi, end-of-summer assembly address. Hongzhi uses the verb of seeing through the two ends.

Occurrences.Kwic: 須是眼清手便的人於此覷破，說成佛也是、說作祖也是，說悟、說見總是。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A late recorded saying comments on Deshan and his attendant and calls for an eye-clear, hand-ready person to see through it. No roster identity was asserted.

Occurrences.Kwic: 各自大家堂中喫茶自由自在免見他時異日被人覷破
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of the Ancient Worthies. The clause gives the passive construction 'be seen through by someone'; the governing speaker was left unlinked.

Occurrences.Kwic: 若有箇性燥底，向他未面壁時一覷覷破，還他這老漢不坐在含元殿裏相見。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A comment on Luzhu's facing-the-wall encounter uses the emphatic one-look construction before the recorded action.

Occurrences.Kwic: 先將世間法一一覷破
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Chaōzong's record tells the assembled laymen first to see through worldly things one by one. No roster identity was asserted.

Occurrences.Kwic: 便向未舉已前一覷覷破
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Miyin's recorded address again uses the emphatic one-look form before something is raised. The master is not present in the linking roster under a safely confirmed name.
